changes.before: Port allocation adds another finite resource. A fixed published TCP port cannot be reused on the same node in one plan. Dynamic ports come from the planner's30000–32767 interval, excluding reservations already seen in the snapshot or selected earlier in the current plan. A port failure can remain reserved in accounting to avoid immediately repeating an observed conflict. This logic concerns node-scoped host bindings; it is not a cluster-wide virtual service address.

changes.before: Now remove only the existing reservation on nodeb in a copied fixture. Both ready nodes become eligible for the first task, but nodeb has more memory remaining after placement and wins that comparison. Its chosen fixed port then prevents the second Atlas task from sharing nodeb, while nodec remains available. Predict two assignments to different nodes before running the changed fixture. This small change demonstrates why a constraint must be applied before a score: a high-scoring node with a conflicting fixed port was previously ineligible, whereas the same node without that reservation can participate. changes.before: The notifier has an explicit set of event types eligible for delivery. Dispatcher.Notify ignores unrelated types, loads sinks and sends to them sequentially. changes.before: Suppose Atlas has two replicas, each requesting 250m CPU and 128Mi memory, and its spec declares one positive published TCP port. The service contributes one service, two replicas,500 millicores,268435456 memory bytes and one public-port declaration. A dynamic declaration with published_port zero does not add that same positive-port count at this boundary. This is declared service usage, not the number of actual host socket bindings.
